title: First-Principles Investigation of Multimodal Toxic Gas Sensing in Carbon-Tuned hBN-Graphene Alloys: Chemiresistive, Work-Function, and Optical Responses
abstract: Compact, reliable, and cost-effective gas sensors have become a highly demanding subject for safety management in the medical sector, chemical manufacturing, food quality monitoring, agriculture, and industrial safety. Hazardous gas emissions need to be controlled and monitored with fast-responsive and highly sensitive sensing devices. A first-principles study employing density functional theory (DFT) was used to investigate the adsorption behavior of Cl2, CO, CO2, NO, NO2, and HCN gas molecules with our proposed alloys, which consisted of hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) and graphene (Gr). The alloy consisting of 22% carbon (BNGr-2) was found to be most competent for sensing Cl2, CO, CO2, and HCN with sufficient adsorption energy, charge transfer, and bandgap alteration. However, NO and NO2 gas molecules showed more engagement with 33% carbon-proportioned alloy (BNGr-3) in terms of adequate gas sensing properties. NOx gases exhibited the most chemiresistive sensitivity towards the adsorbents. Other gases also showed significant chemiresistive sensitivity and distinct selectivity ratios, which would facilitate these alloys as chemiresistive sensors. Besides, noticeable work function variation (~20%) of these systems manifested potential as work function based sensors. Cl2 and NO2 showed strong physical adsorption, while the rest of the gases were weakly to moderately physisorbed, resulting in very short recovery times (10-1 ~ 10-6 seconds). Additionally, the distinctive absorption spectra observed for the gas analyte systems highlighted the potential of the proposed alloys as optical gas sensors. Temperature variation revealed that all gas molecules can be freed from the adsorbent BNGr-2 at 425 K. These findings imply hBN-Gr alloys as promising gas sensors for pollution auditing.
summary: This theoretical study uses DFT to investigate how carbon doping in hBN-Graphene alloys tunes their electronic structure for use as gas sensors. The research identifies optimal alloy compositions for detecting various toxic gases ($	ext{Cl}_2, 	ext{CO}, 	ext{NOx}$, etc.) via chemiresistive, work function, and optical responses. The findings suggest these engineered alloys are highly promising candidates for next-generation environmental monitoring devices.
main_problem: The development of compact, reliable, and cost-effective gas sensors for monitoring hazardous gas emissions in various industrial and safety applications.
main_result: Carbon-tuned hBN-Graphene alloys show promise as multimodal gas sensors, with different carbon ratios optimizing performance for specific gas types ($	ext{NOx}$ for $	ext{BNGr-3}$, $	ext{Cl}_2$ for $	ext{BNGr-2}$).
method: First-principles calculations using Density Functional Theory (DFT) were employed to model gas adsorption and electronic responses.
model_or_system: The physical system consists of hexagonal boron nitride ($	ext{hBN}$) and graphene ($	ext{Gr}$) alloys, where varying carbon content tunes the electronic properties. The study investigates adsorption of $	ext{Cl}_2$, $	ext{CO}$, $	ext{CO}_2$, $	ext{NO}$, $	ext{NO}_2$, and $	ext{HCN}$ onto these alloys.
key_observables: Adsorption energy, charge transfer, bandgap alteration, chemiresistive sensitivity, work function variation ($\sim 20\%$), and distinct optical absorption spectra.
important_parameters: Carbon content (e.g., 22% for $	ext{BNGr-2}$, 33% for $	ext{BNGr-3}$), temperature (up to $425 	ext{ K}$), and gas analyte identity.
main_assumptions: The calculations rely on DFT approximations (GGA with PBE functional) and assume that the observed electronic and chemical changes are indicative of real-world sensor performance.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate optimized geometries, band structures, and density of states (DOS) for the alloys and adsorbed gases, alongside spectral data for different gas analytes.
paper_structure: The paper systematically investigates the effect of varying carbon ratios in hBN-Gr alloys, calculating adsorption energies and electronic properties for multiple toxic gases, and analyzing the resulting chemiresistive, work function, and optical sensing characteristics.
why_interesting: While the primary focus is materials science/chemistry, the use of first-principles methods to predict macroscopic device behavior (sensing) is relevant to theoretical condensed matter physics, particularly in modeling interfacial charge transfer and electronic state changes.
